newsitem.title: USA: New York brings weapons charges against leftists.
newsitem.headline: New York brings weapons charges against leftists.

text.p: Authorities charged three people with criminal weapons possession and issued grand jury subpoenas Wednesday for 35 members of a self-styled leftist group that allegedly turned a Brooklyn house into an arsenal.

The arms cache was discovered Monday night after police were turned away from a brownstone in the Crown Heights neighbourhood when they went to investigate a neighbour's call about possible child abuse.

They returned to the house with a search warrant to find the children involved but instead came upon a disguised closet filled with weapons and ammunition. The children were eventually found next door with no visible signs of abuse.

New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani told a news conference at police headquarters Wednesday that the group called itself the Provisional Party of Communists, also known as the Eastern Services Workers and the National Labour Federation.

"They involved themselves in workers' movements. They had a lot of literature that is all being analysed now. They appear to be connected to other groups outside the city of New York," Giuliani said. He said he had no further details of the group's plans.
The Communist Party, USA said it had no relationship with the group and that it objected to authorities identifying those arrested as "communists."

"The Communist Party, USA has absolutely no relationship with or even knowledge of the existence of the group," it said in a statement. "Any future reference to this group, or individuals in the group as 'communists' will be considered slanderous."

Experts in fringe groups and cults said the 35 people arrested in the house and two connecting ground-floor apartments in adjacent buildings were followers of Eugenio Perente-Ramos, a radical labour organiser who died in March 1995. They said Parente-Ramos had several hundred followers on the East and West coasts but they were not engaged in much serious political activity.

First Deputy Police Commisioner Tosano Simonetti told reporters federal authorities would probably become involved in the investigation. The FBI executed a search warrant at the house in 1984 but no arrests were made.
The 35 people subpoenaed will testify before a grand jury, which will decide whether to bring further charges.

Displayed at the news conference Wednesday were 17 handguns including a .357 Magnum, 27 rifles, five shotguns, one airgun, blackjacks and assorted knives. Also found and shown to reporters were dummy grenades, five pounds of black powder for rifle cartridges, three bulletproof vests, handcuffs, holsters, false identity documents, $42,000 in cash and several personal computers.

Brooklyn District Attorney Charles Hynes said the three women in whose names the house was registered had been charged with criminal possession of a weapon and criminal sale of a weapon. Police identified them as Ann Ribar, 46, Susan Angus, 45, and Diane Garret, 45.

Hynes said that under existing law none of the other members of the group could be charged with weapons possession. But two other people arrested at the house were charged with obstructing government administration. They were identified as Reginald Williams, 45, and William Dobron, 34.
